Currently when I write sSupHom α Prop, the SupSet instance on Prop lands on ConditionallyCompleteLattice.toConditionallyCompletePartialOrder.toSupSet, which is noncomputable, even though the instance I end up using (CompleteLattice Prop) is perfectly computable.

Now I know we generally don't care about computability, but this confused me for a while — in particular, i got a "noncomputable" error for code like this

def toPropOrderIsoDual : sSupHom α Prop ≃o αᵒᵈ := <some (computable) term>

but not for this

def toPropOrderIsoDual := <the same term>

which threw me :/.

I understand there was discussion about taking away the data part of SupSet (eg here), which would fix this (to my understanding). In my case I fixed the issue by adding a shortcut

instance : SupSet Prop := Prop.instCompleteLattice.toSupSet

but would this be something we want to fix in general? This seems like a rare case where the defeq for sSup could be useful.
Yes, shortcut instances to preserve computability is standard practice. Please PR :slight_smile:

Note more generally that it is nonsensical to compute a Prop (what would the bit representation be?), but the computability checker doesn't realise this when the Prop isn't wrapped in a structure (like sSupHom)

You could test if it does by adding

attribute [-instance] Prop.linearOrder Prop.instCompleteLinearOrder in

before your def
thanks! that fixes it :) i'll defer to the more general fix on the PR i suppose

Yaël Dillies said:

Note more generally that it is nonsensical to compute a Prop (what would the bit representation be?), but the computability checker doesn't realise this when the Prop isn't wrapped in a structure (like sSupHom)

right that makes sense (maybe u meant "when the Prop is wrapped ...") — honestly it seemed a little strange that it was computable at all, i mostly wanted to mark it so for symmetry with the sInfHom version, from which it is derived by chaining a bunch of order isos.
